newsitem.title: USA: SEC's Maco warns issuers on fraud prevention plans.
newsitem.headline: SEC's Maco warns issuers on fraud prevention plans.

text.p: Local finance agencies can take specific steps to protect bond issues from federal scrutiny, but no one set of written procedures can fully immunize panels against potential liability, an SEC official said.

Paul Maco, director of Securities and Exchange Commission's Office of Municipal Securities, issued the warning at an Association of Local House Finance Agencies (ALHFA) workshop on SEC's primary and secondary disclosure standards.

Maco was responding to recommendations by panelists on what housing agency boards can do to protect themselves from federal action like the SEC's January 1996 filing of a cease and desist order against Orange County's board of surpervisors for inadequate bond disclosure.

For instance, John Wagner, a bond lawyer with Kutak Rock in Omaha, recommended that boards demand a list of the developers, bond lawyers, and financial advisers participating in their financings, particularly conduit deals.

Boards also should approve or disapprove an offering at a public meeting where they specifically ask bond professionals if there are any potential problems with a financing that could come back to haunt them later, Wagner said.
"And make sure that board minutes reflect the fact that you asked the question because, ultimately, the paper trail is what protects you," Wagner said.

Likewise, Rebecca Yanisch, executive director of the Minneapolis Community Development Agency, urged authorities to make sure that there votes on bond offerings are listed as discussion items at public meetings rather than placed on a "consent," or non-public, calendar.

Maco said that while the recommendations are good ones, the "best set of minutes in the world will not override reality. It all depends on the facts and cirumstances" of an offering whether the SEC decides to investigate, he said.
A board can produce a "nice set of minutes," but if everyone in the room is "winking and nodding" about what is really going on, a written record will not help, Maco said.

John Murphy, ALFHA's executive director, told workshop participants that the association will issue detailed voluntary guidelines by this summer that local housing finance agencies can use to meet disclosure responsibilities.

Richard Martin, a bond attorney with Leonard, Street and Deinard in Minneapolis, said the guidelines will recommend that agencies have their own lawyers and financial advisers on staff rather than hiring consultants.
He said that agencies that are unable to do so should use the same professionals from deal to deal, if possible.
In other recommendations, Wager said finance agency boards should always get a draft of the prospectus before they vote on whether to proceed with a deal.
"Sometimes people don't like to pass prospectuses out," he said. "We think they should."
